title: Microfragment catalog and temporal-locality KV residency coordinator
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: We observe repeated small variations of user prompts (templated slots, punctuation, tokenization differences) creating many near-duplicate KV entries that inflate GPU-resident storage and reduce effective cache hit rate during continuous batching. Interleaved multi-tenant batching exacerbates fragmentation of GPU slabs, increasing OOM pressure and eviction churn.

Goal: Implement a lightweight, GPU-aware microfragment catalog that enables cross-request deduplication and a temporal-locality residency coordinator. The system should: (1) compactly identify microfragment equivalence (syntactic + semantic normalization), (2) score fragments for residency credits based on recency and reuse frequency, (3) integrate with the batch scheduler to co-schedule requests that unlock existing resident fragments, and (4) provide safe multi-tenant isolation and auditability.

High-level approach:
- Fragment normalization: normalize whitespace, canonicalize slot placeholders, and token-length bin to reduce superficial differences. Compute two fingerprints per fragment: a fast content hash for exact matches and a compact semantic fingerprint (64-bit locality-sensitive hash) for fuzzy merges.
- Microfragment catalog: content-addressed index stored off-GPU (compressed), mapping fragment -> residency metadata (resident GPU slab id, residency credit score, last_used_ts, tenant-id). Catalog supports atomic upsert to avoid race conditions when multiple requests attempt to claim the same resident slice.
- Residency coordinator: assign credits to fragments proportional to observed reuse and temporal locality (recency decay window). Credits drive eviction scoring inside the GPU slab allocator: high-credit fragments are pinned longer; low-credit ones are soft-evicted under pressure.
- Batch scheduler integration: extend request admission to consult the catalog. When forming continuous batches, prefer grouping requests that share high-credit fragments to increase shared KV hits and reduce duplicated slab allocations. Scheduler should have a backoff to avoid increasing tail latency.
- Safety and multi-tenant controls: per-tenant catalog namespaces and quota knobs. Consent/PII safeguarding by hashing at the fragment level and optional client-side canonicalization where needed.

Trade-offs and mitigations:
- Fingerprinting CPU overhead: mitigate with async fingerprint workers and sampling for long queries. For small/short prompts we use only fast exact hashes.
- Semantic false positives: keep semantic merges conservative (require both semantic similarity and matching token-length bin). Add a rollback mechanism for mis-merged fragments that detects degradation in log-prob distributions and unmerges in catalog.
- Scheduler-induced latency: implement a soft preference (score boost) rather than strict co-scheduling to avoid blocking requests. Monitor end-to-end latency and abort preference if P95 increases beyond target.

Implementation plan:
1) Spike (2w): offline simulator that replays production traces to measure potential dedupe ratio and estimated GPU-resident savings for different fingerprint thresholds.
2) Prototype (3w): implement microfragment catalog service + residency metadata, a GPU slab residency API, and a scheduler hook for suggestions (no enforcement). Deploy prototype on dev cluster with synthetic workloads.
3) Integration (2w): wire prototype into runtime allocator, implement atomic claim/merge protocol, and add metrics/tracing.
4) Canary (1w): 5% Dedicated traffic with monitoring dashboards, automatic rollback if token-cost or latency regressions occur.
5) Ramp (2w): incremental rollout with tenant safety windows.

Observability and debugging: instrument catalog hit/miss rates, fragment churn rate, slab occupancy heatmap, eviction reason histograms, per-tenant residency credits distribution, and synthesized end-to-end token cost savings. Provide an admin debug API to inspect candidate merges and unmerge history.

Spike notebook + simulator: s3://redwood-traces/kv-simulators/microfragment-spike-2026-02.tar.gz
Initial PR (prototype): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4207

Risks: catalog growth causing DB pressure (mitigate via TTL + compaction), cross-tenant spill if isolation not enforced (mitigate via strong namespace + quotas), and small pathological workloads where dedupe adds cost (monitor and disable per-tenant).

Next steps: produce offline simulator numbers from trace subset 2026-02, implement prototype catalog with atomic claim logic, and schedule a design review with PM and runtime leads for week of 2026-03-15.
acceptance_criteria:
- Offline simulator shows >=15% reduction in unique GPU-resident KV footprint for conversational traces (target 15-30%).
- Prototype can claim/merge microfragments without data races under 100 rps synthetic test.
- Canary demonstrates token-cost reduction >=10% with no more than 5% P95 latency regression vs baseline (rollback if regression >5%).
- No cross-tenant leakage observed in canary; per-tenant quotas respected.
- Relevant metrics and debug views added to Console (catalog hit rate, slab occupancy, eviction reasons).
